questions.q: Forward vs reverse proxy: on whose behalf does each act?
options: Forward proxies serve servers; reverse proxies serve clients
Both act for clients; the word reverse refers to response direction
A forward proxy acts for clients; a reverse proxy fronts servers
Both act for servers; the word forward refers to request direction
questions.explanation: A forward proxy sits next to the client and hides it from the internet; a reverse proxy sits in front of servers and hides them from clients. The direction names whose side it is on.

questions.q: What is TLS termination at a reverse proxy?
options: The proxy decrypts client TLS, then forwards traffic to backends, often re-encrypted
The proxy blocks all encrypted TLS traffic, permitting only unencrypted plaintext HTTP through
The proxy rejects expired certificates and drops those client connections
The proxy tunnels the encrypted bytes untouched through to the backend
questions.explanation: Terminating means the TLS session ends at the proxy, which holds the certificate and decrypts. That plaintext view is what enables L7 routing, caching, and header inspection.

questions.q: What is a common use of a forward proxy in a corporate network?
options: Distributing inbound traffic across the company's public web servers
Terminating TLS for the company's customer-facing website
Caching database query results for internal applications
Filtering and logging employees' outbound internet access
questions.explanation: A forward proxy is the chokepoint for outbound traffic, so it is the natural place to enforce URL policy, log egress, and cache external content. The other options describe reverse proxies.

questions.q: Why does a backend behind a reverse proxy see the proxy's IP as the peer address?
options: NAT at the ISP rewrites all source addresses along the path
The proxy opens its own TCP connection to the backend
The backend's firewall rewrites source headers on arrival
HTTP hides client IP addresses by default for privacy
questions.explanation: A proxy is two separate connections spliced together. The backend's socket peer is whoever dialed it, which is the proxy, so the original client address is simply not on that connection.

questions.q: Which header conventionally carries the original client IP through proxies?
options: X-Forwarded-For, or the standardized Forwarded header
Host, which accumulates a list of every hop the request has traversed
User-Agent, which each proxy appends its address to
Content-Location, which records the request's source
questions.explanation: X-Forwarded-For is the de facto convention, with each proxy appending the address it received from; RFC 7239's Forwarded header standardizes the same idea.

questions.q: What is a sidecar proxy?
options: A standby backup proxy instance that activates only when the main gateway has failed entirely
A browser extension that routes user traffic through a VPN
A single proxy shared by all services running on one physical rack
A per-service proxy deployed alongside each instance, handling its network traffic
questions.explanation: A sidecar runs in the same pod or host as one service instance and intercepts its inbound and outbound traffic, moving mTLS, retries, and telemetry out of application code.

questions.q: Which set of responsibilities typically belongs to a reverse proxy?
options: Compiling the application's source code and serving the resulting build artifacts
Load balancing, TLS termination, caching, and request routing
Managing database transactions on behalf of the application
Allocating virtual machine capacity for backend autoscaling
questions.explanation: These are all cross-cutting edge concerns that apply to every request regardless of application logic, so centralizing them at the proxy keeps backends simpler.

questions.q: What does it mean for a proxy to be transparent?
options: It only forwards HTTPS traffic and never plain unencrypted HTTP
Its entire configuration is stored on disk in human-readable plain text files
Traffic is intercepted without client configuration; clients are unaware
It is engineered to add zero measurable latency to any request
questions.explanation: Transparency refers to client visibility: the network redirects traffic through the proxy, so no proxy settings are configured on the client and it thinks it talks to the origin directly.

questions.q: The backend logs every request as coming from the proxy's IP. What restores real client IPs?
options: Enable TCP keepalive on the proxy so the original source address persists downstream
Have the proxy set X-Forwarded-For and make the backend trust it from that hop
Switch the proxy to UDP transport, which preserves source addresses
Run the backend on the same host so that no proxy hop is needed
questions.explanation: Since the client address is lost at the TCP layer, it must be carried in-band at L7. The backend must also be configured to trust that header only from known proxy addresses.

questions.q: Why is blindly trusting X-Forwarded-For dangerous?
options: The header is encrypted and cannot be validated by backends
Intermediate proxies always strip it, so it never reaches the backend application anyway
Clients can spoof it, defeating IP allowlists and rate limits keyed on it
It doubles the request size, degrading throughput measurably
questions.explanation: It is just a client-settable header. Unless the edge proxy overwrites it and the backend counts hops from a trusted set, an attacker can forge any source IP they like.

questions.q: You need L7 routing at the proxy plus encrypted links to backends. What is the standard setup?
options: Terminate TLS at the edge, then re-encrypt proxy-to-backend (or mTLS via a mesh)
Use full end-to-end TLS passthrough so the proxy never decrypts any client traffic at any point
Encrypt only the requests carrying cookies or authorization headers
Use IPsec tunnels between users and backends, skipping the proxy
questions.explanation: L7 routing requires reading headers, which requires decryption, so passthrough is ruled out. Re-encrypting the upstream leg keeps the internal network confidential.

questions.q: Service mesh sidecars (like Envoy) add what capability, at what cost?
options: Kernel-bypass networking for every service, at the cost of installing custom NIC hardware
Automatic schema validation for APIs, at the cost of slower deploys
Free horizontal scaling of services, at the cost of vendor lock-in
Uniform mTLS, retries, and telemetry, at the cost of extra hops and resource overhead
questions.explanation: A mesh gives every service identical, language-agnostic networking policy without code changes, but each call now traverses two extra proxies burning CPU and memory.

questions.q: A reverse proxy buffers slow client uploads before forwarding them. What does this protect against?
options: Cross-site scripting payloads embedded in multipart uploads
DNS rebinding attacks targeting internal backend services on private networks
Backend workers being tied up by slow clients (slowloris-style exhaustion)
TLS downgrade attacks against resumed client sessions
questions.explanation: Buffering absorbs the slow drip at the proxy, which handles many idle connections cheaply, and only occupies a scarce backend worker once the full request is ready.

questions.q: Why does a backend behind a TLS-terminating proxy need X-Forwarded-Proto?
options: To know the original scheme (https) for redirects and secure cookies despite plain HTTP internally
To choose a response compression codec that matches the client's originally negotiated TLS version
To reject any request that arrived over IPv6 at the edge
To measure the proxy's added latency on each request hop
questions.explanation: The backend sees plain HTTP and would otherwise emit http:// absolute redirects and skip the Secure cookie flag, causing redirect loops and insecure cookies.

questions.q: Why must proxies strip hop-by-hop headers (those listed in Connection)?
options: They contain credentials that must never leave the first hop
They are compressed differently and would corrupt the body length
Keeping them doubles the total header size at every successive hop
They describe one connection only; forwarding them can confuse downstream behavior
questions.explanation: Headers like Connection, Keep-Alive, and Transfer-Encoding govern a single TCP hop. Leaking them onward misrepresents the next connection and is a classic request-smuggling vector.

questions.q: A reverse proxy's health check marks a backend unhealthy. What should the proxy do?
options: Return 500 for the share of traffic that backend would have served
Stop routing to it and redistribute traffic until its checks pass again
Restart the backend process over SSH automatically
Cache the backend's last responses and serve them indefinitely
questions.explanation: The point of health checking is to eject bad instances from the pool so requests go only to healthy ones, then re-admit automatically once checks pass again.

questions.q: A proxy keeps a keepalive pool of 100 connections; the backend's concurrency limit is 80. What happens under burst?
options: The pool renegotiates a fresh TLS handshake per request, tripling CPU usage at the edge
Backends silently drop the keepalive connections, causing DNS storms
The proxy dedupes concurrent identical requests, corrupting responses
Excess in-flight requests exceed the backend limit, causing queuing or 503s
questions.explanation: The proxy's pool size is an implicit concurrency limit. Sizing it above what the backend can serve just moves the queue downstream, where it turns into latency or rejections.

questions.q: A layer-4 proxy forwards raw TCP, losing client IPs. How is client identity commonly preserved?
options: By embedding the client IP into the TCP sequence numbers
PROXY protocol: a preamble carrying original addresses, understood by the backend
By reusing the client's ephemeral port on the backend connection
By GRE-tunneling every single flow so the original headers stay intact end to end
questions.explanation: At L4 there are no HTTP headers to use, so HAProxy's PROXY protocol prepends a small fixed header with the source and destination addresses before the first byte of payload.

questions.q: A shared proxy fleet fronts 200 services; one bad rewrite rule loops requests back to the proxy. Blast radius and guard?
options: Only that one service breaks; loops are confined by per-service TLS certificates
Nothing breaks; proxies detect forwarding loops via TCP TTL automatically
The whole fleet can saturate; guard with loop-detection headers (Via) and hop limits
Only DNS suffers; the correct fix is lowering record TTLs during incidents
questions.explanation: A loop multiplies requests against a shared connection and worker pool, so one misconfigured route starves all 200 tenants. Via or hop-count checks break the cycle early.

questions.q: What is the realistic cost of running mTLS everywhere via sidecar proxies?
options: Extra CPU for crypto, added per-hop latency, and cert-rotation operational burden
No measurable cost, since modern NICs offload all TLS work in hardware
Purely a memory cost: every sidecar must hold the complete mesh topology in RAM
Doubled bandwidth usage, because mTLS encrypts each packet twice
questions.explanation: Handshakes and record encryption cost CPU, each sidecar hop adds latency, and short-lived certificates need automated issuance and rotation or the mesh fails closed.
